note.question: What determines the design of fair, efficient, budget-balanced, and implementable bidding mechanisms for observable queues?
note.overview: The model considers the problem of resolving ad hoc unpredictable congestion in environments where customers have private time valuations. We investigate the design of fair, efficient, budget-balanced, and implementable bidding mechanisms for observable queues. The paper's primary motivation comes from merging in algorithmic traffic, i.e., a driver wishing to merge in a relatively dense platoon of vehicles in a coordinated and efficient way, using intervehicle communication and micropayments, akin to an arriving customer trading for position in a single-server observable queue.

We are interested in the case where the free-lane drivers form a relatively dense platoon (i.e., the gaps between them are small enough so that a merging necessarily disrupts the flow of traffic on the free lane, causing delays to some vehicles).
The default option of the merging driver, in case she cannot come to an agreement with any free-lane driver, is to merge at the end of the platoon.

components.explanation: Similarly, in settings where virtual queueing is prevalent (e.g., call centers or even make-to-order manufacturing), the entity that owns or manages the virtual queue can divulge real-time information about its length and the positions of different customers in it, thus turning an initially unobservable queue into an observable one.

conditions: Similarly, in settings where virtual queueing is prevalent (e.g., call centers or even make-to-order manufacturing), the entity that owns or manages the virtual queue can divulge real-time information about its length and the positions of different customers in it, thus turning an initially unobservable queue into an observable one.

One can view the aforementioned merging scenario as a customer joining a single-server observable queue, something that makes our modeling framework and results relevant to a variety of settings in service operations management.
Queueing is de facto observable in physical queues (e.g., people waiting in line for transportation and government services) or for infrastructure, such as ports, airports, canals, etc.
The average of the delay is c E[Sb] time units, where Sb is the distribution of the service time of the arriving customer, assumed to be public information.

components.label: The T2H Bidding Mechanism
components.explanation: Essentially, free-lane drivers are price takers with veto power; they either accept the offered payment and let the driver merge at some point ahead of them, or they veto further progress and the merge happens immediately behind them.

components.formal: Decision rule: Essentially, free-lane drivers are price takers with veto power; they either accept the offered payment and let the driver merge at some point ahead of them, or they veto further progress and the merge happens immediately behind them.
conditions: We assume that a platform documents the bids and enforces the rules and payments implied by the mechanism.

In the final queue order, no queuer should have suffered a net negative externality after payments are made; in other words, net utility postmerging should be no less than the one before it for every agent.

conditions: As we saw in Section 4.2, the perfect information social optimum, defined as US maxiUi, is not an informative measure to compare against the proposed bidding mechanisms, as it assumes knowledge of the private time valuations of drivers.
We define the SOPI as follows; consider an altruistic merging driver who knows only her private time valuation as well as the joint distribution of time valuations of free-lane drivers.
We denote by ̄b ∗ i the solution to the optimization problem (i.e., the bid that the merging driver makes to driver i on the platoon in order to maximize the expected social welfare of the platoon).
